summary: This document discusses issues that arise when RTP sessions span UTC leap seconds. It updates RFC 3550 by describing how RTP senders and receivers should behave in the presence of a leap second.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes the world's clocks add an extra second. This explains how audio and video streams should cope without getting confused.

subtitle: How RTP streams tied to wall-clock time should behave when UTC adds a leap second.

tldr.problem: RTP streams that are tied to a wall clock need smooth, continuous time, but UTC leap seconds make wall clocks jump, freeze or repeat, so senders and receivers can disagree about timestamps.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates RFC 3550 with recommendations: use a clock without leap seconds if possible, otherwise recognize leap seconds, avoid NTP timestamps in the affected second, and skip sender report timestamps near a positive leap second.
tldr.outcome: Streams that are not tied to a wall clock need no changes. Wall-clock-referenced streams that follow the advice avoid playback interruptions around a leap second.

sections.title: Why Leap Seconds Matter to RTP
sections.content:
Some media applications tie an RTP stream to a wall-clock time (an absolute date and time). They do this through the NTP timestamp field in the sender report (SR), which maps RTP timestamps to the wall clock. Playout time is then referenced to that wall clock.

Smooth playout needs a smooth and continuous time base, but wall clocks that include leap seconds may not render them smoothly. RFC 7164 updates RFC 3550 with recommendations for rendering such streams smoothly.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a movie that is timed by a wall clock. If the clock suddenly hiccups, the movie could stutter. This RFC explains how to avoid that.

sections.title: What a Leap Second Is
sections.content:
International Atomic Time (TAI) is the scientific time standard, while civil time follows the rotation of the Earth. In 1972, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) was redefined in terms of TAI and leap seconds were introduced to keep UTC in step with the Earth's rotation.

Leap seconds always occur at the end of the UTC day, not local time. They can add a second (a positive leap second) or skip one (a negative leap second). They are typically not scheduled more than six months in advance, and since 1972 all of them have been in June or December and all have been positive.
sections.plainLanguage: The Earth spins a little unevenly, so sometimes the world's clocks add one extra second to catch up. It is like adding one more tick to the end of a day.

sections.title: How Different Clocks Handle It
sections.content:
Clocks disagree about what to show during a positive leap second. UTC shows a 61st second, 23:59:60. NTP freezes or slows the clock for one second just before the last second of the day, so that last second lasts two real seconds and timestamp accuracy suffers. POSIX requires that leap seconds be omitted, with every day having 86,400 seconds; many systems repeat the last second, which makes a timestamp in it ambiguous. Others copy NTP, and some warp time by slightly changing the length of a second.

The RFC's example is the positive leap second of June 30, 2012, when the TAI-UTC offset changed from 34 to 35 seconds, shown for an 8 kHz audio stream.
sections.plainLanguage: When the extra second arrives, one clock counts it, one repeats a second, and one pauses. Everyone ends up showing the same time afterwards, but in the middle they disagree.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong at the Receiver
sections.content:
Timestamps made during a leap second can be ambiguous, or read differently by a sender and a receiver, or by different receivers. Without advance knowledge of the leap-second schedule, NTP servers and clients may become offset by exactly one second from their UTC reference, until all participants get a time update. Depending on the system, that can last from a few seconds to a few days.

The offset may make a receiver think packets arrive after they should be played, or make it buffer data an additional second. Either can interrupt playback. Some receivers resynchronize on their own, and may need to resynchronize again once the offset is resolved.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sender thinks it is one second later than the receiver does, the receiver may play sounds too late or wait too long, and the music hiccups.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Senders and receivers not referenced to a wall clock are unaffected and need no accommodation. Clocks on a TAI-based timescale, such as IEEE 1588 and GPS, do not include leap seconds, which simplifies things. NTP time, operating system clocks and other UTC-referenced systems do include them. What matters is the timescale used, not how the time is delivered.

All participants generating or consuming timestamps tied to a leap-second-bearing reference MUST recognize leap seconds and SHOULD have a working channel for leap-second notifications, such as the Leap Indicator in the NTP header. Generating or using NTP timestamps during the whole last second of a day with a scheduled positive leap second SHOULD be avoided. That period lasts two real seconds. Negative leap seconds need no special treatment. POSIX clocks that warp time SHOULD not be used to timestamp RTP streams.
sections.plainLanguage: If your clock never adds extra seconds, you are fine. If it does, you must know when the extra second is coming, and you should avoid stamping things during the confusing moment.

sections.title: Sender Reports and Playout
sections.content:
Senders and receivers should avoid using sender reports to synchronize clocks near a leap second and rely on their internal clocks until it has passed. Senders using a leap-second-bearing reference SHOULD NOT generate sender reports with an originating NTP timestamp near a positive leap second. To keep the RTCP schedule steady and avoid unintended timeouts, they MAY send receiver reports instead.

Receivers consuming such timestamps SHOULD ignore timestamps in sender reports generated near a positive leap second. Both sides MAY assume a positive leap second occurs at the end of the last day of every month. For playout, receivers SHOULD take both positive and negative leap seconds into account when working out playout time from RTP timestamps.
sections.plainLanguage: Near the extra second, senders skip the clock-setting messages and just keep their own time. Receivers ignore any such messages that do show up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Wall-clock-referenced RTP streams add an attack vector compared to self-clocking streams: manipulating the wall clock at the sender or receiver can disrupt streaming. A stream can also be disrupted by blocking or delaying leap-second notice to one participant, or by tricking a participant into believing a leap second is scheduled when it is not.

These vulnerabilities already exist in RFC 3550, and the new recommendations neither heighten nor diminish them. Integrity of the leap-second schedule is the job of the operating system and the time distribution mechanism, which are outside the scope of this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy messes with your clock or hides the news about the extra second, your stream can break. This RFC does not make that worse or better.
